- Bound direct matches with `--limit 60` rather than piping to `head`, which can silently discard relevant output and errors.

Required: one successful `slopdex map` before grep/read; other slopdex navigation is blocked.
Checkout and symbol vectors are ready; never override root/index/config.
For Go discovery add --ignore-errors -g '*.go' -g '!**/*_test.go'.

tasks.prompt: Investigate the active Go-native implementation in this checkout. Identify three implementation functions: the one that interprets the package's export map for the requested root or subpath; the one that selects an exact or expanding subpath key and extracts the matched portion; and the recursive one that interprets the selected target and attempts resolution. Explain the flow between them, how wildcard precedence is determined, how conditions and arrays are traversed, and how an explicit null target differs from an unsuccessful alternative. Include where target paths are validated and where a matched target becomes a file lookup. Do not modify code.

tasks.prompt: Investigate the active Go-native implementation in this checkout. tasks.prompt: Investigate the active Go-native implementation in this checkout. An editor request captures snapshot S, returns deferred work, and later prepares auto-imports from S while an unrelated edit can make snapshot T canonical. Identify exactly five implementation functions by these mandatory roles: (1) the request wrapper that lends a referenced snapshot and language service to a callback and transfers cleanup into returned deferred work; (2) the host-level derivation routine that prepares auto-imports for a document using the supplied base snapshot's filesystem and overlays without adopting the result; (3) the session-level bridge that obtains the derived snapshot's default project, handles its absence, and queues possible background adoption before returning a language service; (4) the mutex-protected adoption routine that accepts or discards the derived snapshot according to whether its base is still current; and (5) final snapshot disposal that releases program-level resources only when no snapshot still owns the program. Explain the causal call and ownership flow with declaration citations and supporting source evidence, distinguishing the request's reference to S, the derived snapshot's initial reference, language-service reachability, and shared-program ownership. Compare adoption before T exists with rejection after T is current; account for a callback error, a callback with no deferred work, deferred work returning a cancellation error, and failure to find a default project in the derived snapshot. Assume returned deferred work is actually invoked. Does canceling the request itself cancel the already-enqueued adoption, and does rejecting adoption invalidate a language service already returned from the derived snapshot? Explain the relevant contexts and resource lifetimes rather than inferring ownership from object reachability. Finally, contrast a discarded snapshot sharing a program with another live snapshot against the last snapshot owning that program, including ordinary parsed files, mapped output bundles, supplemental files, and checker-pool cleanup. Do not modify code.
tasks.title: Request snapshot ownership when auto-import preparation loses an adoption race

tasks.prompt: Investigate the active Go-native implementation in this checkout. A workspace package is reachable through two dependency-directory symlinks to the same realpath. Its exports change while another package remains clean, and a request asks for auto-imports using an existing registry. Identify exactly five implementation functions by these mandatory roles: (1) the registry scheduler that decides full rebuild versus package-granular update, performs parallel discovery and unique-realpath extraction with type-package fallback, and installs successful bucket results; (2) the granular dependency-bucket updater that replaces dirty-package exports and repairs package-file, path, ambient-module, and entrypoint associations; (3) the word-prefix lookup index's filtered-copy routine that compacts retained entries and remaps character posting lists; (4) the language-service gate that checks preparation for the importing file, canonicalizes supplemental files for that check, and refuses an unprepared registry; and (5) the view's common bucket-query routine that excludes self-imports, applies dependency accessibility, and handles nearer-package shadowing while traversing ancestors. Cite declarations and supporting evidence for the causal flow from dirty state to extraction, immutable replacement, readiness checking, and visible candidates. Explain why the two symlinks can share extraction work while still needing separate bucket installations, and distinguish a main package with usable entrypoints from one requiring the corresponding type-package fallback. Compare a known dirty workspace package with an unclassified dependency change, a changed dependency set, and an expanded recursive-directory-traversal requirement; show which force a full rebuild. Explain how old snapshots retain their indexes, why filtering entries without remapping posting lists would corrupt lookups, and how removed package entrypoints are removed from the registry-wide map. Contrast cancellation before a granular updater starts with a successful extraction and installation: determine from actual error checks which old bucket can remain and how the preparation gate reacts, without assuming all canceled operations roll back atomically. Finally, compare no parseable ancestor package metadata with parseable metadata containing no dependencies, a package directly imported despite not being declared there, and a nearer same-named package with no indexed exports; can an outer package supply candidates in the last case? Do not modify code.
tasks.title: Granular export-cache refresh under shared extraction, cancellation, and package shadowing

tasks.prompt: Investigate the active Go-native implementation in this checkout. A dynamic content mapper watches a configuration file and has produced a cached canonical-plus-supplemental output bundle. The watched configuration changes while the original source text stays identical, and concurrent project construction can request that same source again. Identify exactly five implementation functions by these mandatory roles: (1) the project-collection helper that decides whether watched paths or a refresh-all request affect a mapper project, refreshes it, and removes single-file-update eligibility; (2) the mapper project lease's refresh routine that closes opened remote project handles under lifecycle/state locks and marks them for reopening; (3) the host routine that lazily opens a remote project, validates dynamic versus static configuration identity and watched-file contracts, and commits successful project metadata; (4) the editor compiler-host routine that obtains a mapped source-file bundle through the identity- and locale-sensitive cache, binds a newly produced bundle, and checks supplemental filename collisions; and (5) the generic reference-counted acquisition routine that serializes production for a cache key, reuses successful values, and removes speculative entries on production failure. Explain the causal call and state flow with declaration citations and supporting identity/key evidence. Compare a watched-path hit, an unrelated path, and refresh-all; include the early exits when no program or watched-file set exists. Does a failed remote close leave the local entry opened, and does the project helper stop invalidation on that error? Contrast reopening with the same configuration identity against reopening with a different identity while source bytes and parse options are unchanged, then change only diagnostic locale. Explain what shares or separates cached bundles and why a static mapper returning a configuration identity or watched files, a dynamic mapper returning an empty identity, and a relative watched filename are rejected. For two concurrent misses for the same cache key, distinguish successful production from a first production failure and explain whether the waiter can observe a cached failed value. Finally, compare a transformation error with a physical-file collision at a compiler-assigned supplemental filename: show where cache acquisition is undone, why collision checking also matters on a cache hit, and why reference ownership is for the output bundle rather than each supplemental file independently. Do not modify code.
tasks.title: Dynamic mapper reopening, identity changes, and successful-output bundle ownership

tasks.prompt: Investigate the active Go-native implementation in this checkout. A derived class compiled to ES2015 uses standard decorators, a decorated computed-name auto-accessor with a side-effecting name expression, a private instance method called by a field initializer, and a constructor parameter property. Its explicit super call is inside a try block. Decorators register value initializers and extra instance initializers. Compare assignment-style and define-style public fields, then a fieldless variant in which a decorated instance method still registers extra initializers. Identify exactly five implementation functions by these semantic roles: (1) the script-target dispatcher whose composed transform definitions establish the decorator-before-field stage order; (2) the decorator-stage property visitor that wraps values, consumes earlier pending initializers, queues this member's extra initializers, and expands decorated auto-accessors; (3) the decorator-stage constructor visitor that drains remaining instance initializers and places them around the discovered super-call path; (4) the field-stage constructor-body builder that orders private-method branding, parameter properties, and ordinary field initialization while preserving the super-call location; and (5) the field-stage property-expression worker that selects private storage, assignment, or property definition and recovers parameter-property values through original-node metadata. Trace the handoff through transformed nodes, initializer queues, generated-name reuse, and emit-context metadata, identifying supporting call edges with source evidence. Explain which initializer runs before which field value, why a member's extra initializers must not run before that member's own initialization, and how the final queue is handled when there is no later field. Show how the computed name is evaluated once despite expansion into several declarations. Explain why private-method branding must precede field initializers and why moving inserted statements outside the super-containing try block changes failure behavior. Analyze the counterfactuals of reversing the transform stages, dropping original-node associations, or overwriting a parameter-property initializer without preserving decorator effects. Limit claims about receiver and exception semantics to what this checkout implements. Do not modify code.
tasks.title: Decorator initializer queues crossing the class-field lowering boundary

tasks.prompt: Investigate the active Go-native implementation in this checkout. During inference into a homomorphic mapped type, the checker must reconstruct an input type from source property values. Compare a readonly array, a readonly tuple with optional elements, a partially inferable object containing a context-sensitive member, and a source with neither eligible properties nor a string index signature. Now let both the source and mapped template recursively produce newer instantiations sharing recursion identities, and repeat the same source/target/constraint request after the first attempt was suppressed. Identify exactly five implementation functions by these semantic roles: (1) the reverse-type constructor that checks source eligibility, eagerly reconstructs arrays and tuples, and leaves ordinary objects as lazy reverse-mapped shells; (2) the reverse-inference coordinator that keys memoization by three type identities, maintains separate source and target stacks, and saves/restores expansion flags; (3) the worker that treats the constraint's indexed access as an inference variable, infers against the mapped template, and widens the result or falls back; (4) the shared deep-nesting classifier that uses recursion identities, intersections, and the ordering of type identities rather than stack length alone; and (5) the mapped-template accessor that lazily adds optionality, instantiates the template with its mapper, and caches it. Explain the call/dataflow edges, including the supporting lazy member-resolution path for object shells. Distinguish both-sided expansion from one-sided expansion and describe exactly what is cached when the worker is skipped. Can the first suppressed attempt and a later cache hit return different representations of failure, and where are those normalized for properties or collection elements? Explain tuple optionality reversal and readonly preservation, why the template must reflect its instantiated mapper, and why restoring stack/flag state prevents one sibling property from inheriting another's expansion state. Analyze the counterfactuals of treating every deep stack as recursion or ignoring the constraint in the cache key. Cite implementation evidence rather than assuming all recursive types are rejected. Do not modify code.
tasks.title: Reverse-mapped inference under recursive expansion and cached failure
